## Findings (with sources)

### 1) I cannot directly access or read your inbox, so I can’t summarize “the emails you received last week” unless you provide the email content or export it.
- I did not find any source in the available corpus indicating I have access to a user’s Gmail/Outlook mailbox contents by default, nor any mechanism in this chat context to fetch your email automatically. *(Gap: no inbox access / no email data provided — therefore no per-email summaries can be produced yet.)*

### 2) How to gather “last week’s emails” in Gmail (search + narrow by date)
- Gmail supports searching with operators like `after:` and `before:` using dates in `YYYY/MM/DD`, plus other operators like `newer_than:` / `older_than:` and `label:` / `in:`.  
  Source: Google Gmail Help, “Refine searches in Gmail” (search operators including date operators). https://support.google.com/mail/answer/7190

**Practical implication:** you can pull “last week” by using `after:YYYY/MM/DD before:YYYY/MM/DD` (recommended for a specific week range) or `newer_than:7d` (last 7 days, not aligned to calendar weeks).  
Source: same Gmail Help page above. https://support.google.com/mail/answer/7190

### 3) How to gather “last week’s emails” in Outlook on the web (filtering by date range)
- Outlook on the web provides filtering options including date-based filtering (e.g., “Date” filters such as “This week”, “Last week”, etc., depending on UI/version) via the filter menu.  
  Source: Microsoft Support page describing filtering and sorting messages in Outlook on the web (includes filtering by date). https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/use-filters-to-sort-and-search-your-inbox-in-outlook-on-the-web-4d8e6bfe-9e15-4f3b-bb1e-8d4c0e2cc1fc

**What I did not find:** a single Microsoft page that guarantees the exact label “Last week” exists in all Outlook versions/clients (classic Outlook desktop vs new Outlook vs Outlook on the web). Microsoft’s UI varies; the general capability to filter by date is documented, but exact menu wording can differ.  
Source: same page above (general filter capability, not exact label). https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/use-filters-to-sort-and-search-your-inbox-in-outlook-on-the-web-4d8e6bfe-9e15-4f3b-bb1e-8d4c0e2cc1fc

### 4) Determining “which ones need a reply” requires criteria (unanswered, direct questions, requests, etc.) and/or metadata like “Replied/Answered” status
- In Gmail, you can use search operators like `is:unread`, `from:`, `to:`, and other qualifiers to narrow down messages likely needing attention (e.g., unread).  
  Source: Gmail Help “Refine searches in Gmail”. https://support.google.com/mail/answer/7190

**What I did not find:** a Gmail operator that reliably means “needs reply” or “unreplied” across all accounts; Gmail doesn’t natively tag “needs reply” unless you use stars/labels/tasks/workflows. The help page lists many operators, but “needs reply” is not a built-in search operator there.  
Source: Gmail Help “Refine searches in Gmail” (operator list). https://support.google.com/mail/answer/7190

## Findings (with sources)

### (1) Authoritative Microsoft Support source: Outlook (web) search/filter by date + exact date-format requirements (with quotes)
I found an official Microsoft Support article that explicitly says Outlook on the web search filters include **date ranges**, and (in the same article, under AQS) it states the **required date format** and gives examples for **relative dates like “last week.”**

- Quote (Outlook on the web): “You can use Search filters to refine your search with options like … **date ranges** …” Source: Microsoft Support, *Search Mail and People in Outlook on the web* https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/outlook/search-mail-and-people-in-outlook-on-the-web

- Quote (classic Outlook on the web section / AQS table):
  - “**Sent**: … You can search for a specific date or a range of dates separated by two dots (..). You can also search for relative dates: **today … this week … last week** …”
  - “Important: **Date searches must be entered in month/day/year format: MM/DD/YYYY.**”
  - “**Received** … You can use the same search terms as for Sent.”
  Source: Microsoft Support, *Search Mail and People in Outlook on the web* https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/outlook/search-mail-and-people-in-outlook-on-the-web

**Concrete implication:** In Outlook on the web, you can search using AQS like `received:last week` or `received:01/01/2017..01/31/2017`, and Microsoft documents that date entries must be `MM/DD/YYYY` in that context. Source: same as above.

---

# Weekly email summaries (last week) & which need replies

## What I can do (and what I need from you)
I can summarize your emails from last week and tell you which ones need a reply, but I **can’t access your inbox directly in this chat**. To proceed, you’ll need to **paste** the emails (or excerpts) or **export** them and share the relevant text.

## How to pull “last week” messages

### Gmail (search operators)
Google documents Gmail search operators for date ranges. Examples shown include:
- `after:2004/04/16`
- `before:2004/04/18`
- `after:2004/04/16 before:2004/04/18`

These examples appear under “Search for emails received during a certain time period.”

Use that same pattern with your last-week date range.

**Source:** Google Gmail Help — *Refine searches in Gmail* https://support.google.com/mail/answer/7190

### Outlook on the web (AQS search)
Microsoft documents that Outlook on the web search supports date filtering and relative date terms:
- “You can use Search filters to refine your search with options like … **date ranges** …”
- For date search terms: you can use relative dates such as “**today … this week … last week** …”
- “Important: **Date searches must be entered in month/day/year format: MM/DD/YYYY.**”
- The article indicates **Received** can use the same kinds of search terms as **Sent**.

**Source:** Microsoft Support — *Search Mail and People in Outlook on the web* https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/outlook/search-mail-and-people-in-outlook-on-the-web

## Privacy-preserving ways to share emails with me

### Gmail: export then copy only what’s needed
Google states you can export Gmail data and that the download includes “Message content,” “Message headers,” and “Attachments.” You can export, then locally redact, then paste only the relevant text here.

**Source:** Google Gmail Help — *Export your data from Gmail* https://support.google.com/mail/answer/10016932

### Outlook: save/download message or print to PDF
Microsoft documents options to:
- “Save as” (new Outlook)
- “Download” (Outlook on the web / Outlook.com)
- Print to PDF via Microsoft Print To PDF

You can save/download/print locally, redact, then paste excerpts here.

**Source:** Microsoft Support — *Save an Outlook message as a .eml file, a PDF file, or as a draft* https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/outlook/mail/save-an-outlook-message-as-a-eml-file-a-pdf-file-or-as-a-draft

## How I will decide “needs a reply” (practical framework)
There isn’t a universal “needs reply” flag documented as a standard across email systems. Once you provide the messages, I’ll label each email **Reply needed: Yes/No** (and optionally High/Med/Low priority) using these consistent criteria:

1) **Direct ask**: a question, request for info, approval, decision, or action.
2) **You’re the owner**: you’re directly addressed or explicitly assigned.
3) **Time-sensitive**: deadline/date/time window, or it blocks someone else.
4) **Thread status**: you haven’t responded to the latest message where a response is expected.
5) **No-reply cases**: pure FYI, newsletters/notifications/receipts, or someone else already answered conclusively.

## What to paste (so I can summarize and flag replies)
Paste 5–15 emails at a time in this format (redact as needed):

**Email 1**
- Subject:
- From:
- Date:
- Body (or key excerpt):
- Already replied? (yes/no/unsure):

**Email 2**
- Subject:
- From:
- Date:
- Body (or key excerpt):
- Already replied? (yes/no/unsure):

Once you paste them, I’ll return:
- 1–2 sentence summary per email/thread
- “Reply needed?” + why
- (Optional) a suggested one-paragraph reply draft for each “Yes”

## Conclusions
- I can’t summarize your last week emails without you providing the email text (pasted or exported excerpts).
- Gmail and Outlook on the web both support finding last-week messages via date/relative-date search (Gmail via `after:`/`before:` examples; Outlook on the web via AQS including “last week,” with MM/DD/YYYY date format).
- After you share the messages, I can classify which need replies using a consistent, practical framework (direct asks, ownership, deadlines, and whether you’ve already responded).

- Google Gmail Help — *Refine searches in Gmail* https://support.google.com/mail/answer/7190
- Google Gmail Help — *Export your data from Gmail* https://support.google.com/mail/answer/10016932
- Microsoft Support — *Search Mail and People in Outlook on the web* https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/outlook/search-mail-and-people-in-outlook-on-the-web
